## Task 2 of the robustness study {#task-2-in-the-analysts-own-words .smaller}

::: {.claimcard .small}
- produce a single, main result in terms of statistical families of z-, t-, F-, or $\chi^2$ tests (or their alternative or non-parametric versions).
- disregard contextual variables related to the EU policies and party EU salience and party EU positions indexes in your analysis.
- use the **positive non-materialist form of EU framing** in your analysis.
- use the **unemployment rate** as the measure for poor economic performance in your analysis.
:::

::: {.small}
Four instructions, quoted from my own Task 2 report. Everything else – estimator, sample, weighting, functional form, how you build the scale – was left to us.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The robustness study was designed to fix just enough to make the numbers comparable and to leave the rest free, so that what remained would be a measurement of **analytical variability itself**.
:::

::: notes
This is, word for word, what the robustness study asked of us in its second task, copied from the report that I filed: one main result as a z, t, F or chi-squared test, no contextual variables on EU policies or on the salience and positions of the parties, the positive non-materialist form of EU framing, which the paper calls the cosmopolitan dimension, and the unemployment rate as the measure of poor economic performance. Everything else was left open, the estimator, the sample, the weighting, the functional form, and even the construction of the scale from its items. [advance] The study fixed just enough to make five numbers comparable and left the rest free, so that what remained would measure analytical variability itself, and each point left open is a place where five competent people could legitimately part company, as we did.
:::

## What the instructions assume {#what-those-three-instructions-assume .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **'A single, main result'** assumes that one test statistic can stand for the claim, and leaves its degrees of freedom to the software of each analyst
- **'The positive non-materialist form'** is the cosmopolitan scale of the paper. It assumes that the five items form one scale, and that the summary used in the paper, each respondent's share of mentions, is the right one; a mean, a sum or a factor score would all be defensible
- **'The unemployment rate'** assumes that the claim is about unemployment. The abstract of the paper says "poor economic performances" – which also names GDP growth
- **'Disregard contextual variables'** of EU policy and party positions removes the variables of Model 2. Read literally, it leaves the rest of Model 1 to the analyst, yet four of the five fitted unemployment alone
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these is wrong. Each one is a **decision**, made for you, that a different study could reasonably have made differently.
:::

::: notes
Each instruction rests on an assumption. A single main result assumes that one test statistic can stand for the claim, and it leaves the degrees of freedom to the software of each analyst, which is where the conversion went wrong for one of us. The positive non-materialist form takes for granted that the five items form one scale, summarised as a share of mentions, although a mean, a sum or a factor score would be defensible. 'The unemployment rate' assumes that the claim is about unemployment, while "poor economic performances" names GDP growth just as clearly, and in the free task all five of us used a GDP measure. The last instruction removes the variables of Model 2 and, read literally, leaves the individual controls, growth and the education interactions to the analyst, which four of the five dropped. [advance] Each instruction is a decision, made for you, that another study could reasonably have made differently.
:::

## Analyst no. 6 {#you-are-analyst-no.-6 .smaller}

::: {.big}
- Aim 1: **reproduce** one of the recorded results
:::

::: {.small}
The first row rests on the panel of Hands-on 2, `europeanisation_cy.csv`: 270 country-years, the framing scales as cell means, `unemp`, `growth`, the respondent count `n_cy` and `bailout`.

| Analyst | Data | Model | Recorded in the robustness study |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| C6HJR | the country-year panel, 270 country-years | fixed effects for country and year | t = −3.804 on 233 df |
| KQXUE | a panel of its own, 270 country-years | a fixed effect for each country | t = −7.169 on 242 df |
| 018OL | 420 cells of country, year and wave | random intercepts for country, year and wave | t = −1.206 on 396.9 df |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
KEVF1 and PRL47 fitted their models on respondents, so their reproduction needs the respondent file built from your own GESIS downloads.
:::

::: notes
Your first job as the sixth analyst is a reproduction. The robustness study recorded a result for each of the five of us, and three of those results rest on means of countries or of cells, which may be published, so that they reproduce from files that you already have. Mine is on the country-year panel that you opened in Hands-on 2, with fixed effects for country and year; KQXUE built a panel of its own and gave each country a fixed effect; and 018OL averaged cells of a country in one wave and fitted random intercepts. Choose one of the three. [advance] The other two analysts worked on several hundred thousand respondents, and a reproduction of their results needs the respondent file, which only your own GESIS download can give you. Whichever analyst you choose, the question is the one at the heart of reproducibility, whether the recorded number comes back from the data and the model.
:::
